unit.title: Leisure & Belonging
unit.through_line: A 'third place' is a public place — not home, not school — where you feel you belong. The unit moves through four settings: Study Cafés, the 24-Hour Konbini, Indoor Worlds (malls), and The Disappearing Hangout (gentrification/exclusion).

reading_passages.title: The Café That Never Asks You to Leave
reading_passages.topic: Study Cafés (Seoul/Bangkok study-café culture; pay-by-time; loyalty model; a mild for/against close)
reading_passages.body:
In Seoul, a "study café" looks nothing like an ordinary coffee shop. There are no sofas and no background chatter — just long desks, soft lamps, a power socket at every seat, and rows of students with headphones on. The idea spread quickly across Asia, and today similar cafés are common in Bangkok, where they fill up fastest during exam season.

The appeal is simple: space. Many students live in small flats with noisy younger siblings, and school libraries close early. A study café stays open late — some in Bangkok do not lock their doors until midnight — and charges by time rather than by drink. A typical rate is around 60 baht an hour, often with free refills of water, tea or weak coffee.

Lalita, 17, comes three or four times a week. "At home I get distracted within ten minutes," she says. "Here everyone is working, so I work too. It's quieter than the library, and nobody rushes you." That last point matters. In an ordinary café there is often an unwritten rule — one drink buys you about two hours before a waiter starts hovering. Study cafés remove that pressure completely.

For owners, the model is steady rather than spectacular. "Students don't spend much on each visit," explains one Bangkok café owner, "but they come back again and again, and they bring their friends." Roughly seven in ten of his customers are under twenty. He keeps the prices low and the wifi fast, and trusts that loyalty will do the rest.

Not everyone is convinced the trend is healthy. Some teachers worry that paying to study turns concentration into something only wealthier students can afford. Others point out that, for a teenager with nowhere quiet to go, 60 baht for a calm afternoon may be the cheapest, kindest deal in the city.

reading_passages.title: My Corner
reading_passages.topic: Study Cafés — a first-person 'reading for feeling' text (atmosphere, belonging; contrast morning/afternoon)
reading_passages.body:
There is a small, slightly crooked table in the back-left corner of the café on Soi 7, and for almost a year now it has been mine.

In the morning the place is pale and sleepy. Thin grey light leans through the window, the espresso machine clears its throat, and the only sound is the soft tick of someone's laptop keys. By four o'clock everything has changed. The narrow room fills with the warm smell of toasted bread, the low hum of a dozen overlapping conversations, and a golden, dusty light that makes even the chipped cups look beautiful. I like it best then.

My corner has a wobble in one leg and a long pale scar across the wood, where someone years ago pressed too hard with a pen. The seat is too low and the cushion has gone flat. None of that matters. From there I can see the door, the street, and the old woman who sells flower garlands on the pavement opposite — and nobody can see my screen.

I come here to read, to wait, to do nothing in particular. The owner no longer asks what I want; he simply nods, and a few minutes later a small, strong, sweetened coffee appears at my elbow. I have never told him my name. He has never told me his. And yet, sliding into that uneven chair with the afternoon noise rising around me, I feel something I never feel at home or at school: I feel, completely and quietly, that I belong here.

reading_passages.title: The Shop That Became a Living Room
reading_passages.topic: The 24-Hour Konbini (Japan/Thailand convenience stores as social space; access, cost, ritual; for/against)
reading_passages.body:
In Japan they are called konbini; in Thailand, most people just say "the 7-Eleven." Whatever the name, the 24-hour convenience store has quietly turned into something its designers never planned: an unofficial social space for young people.

The reasons start with access. A konbini never closes. While cafés shut and libraries lock their doors, the convenience store stays lit and open through the night, which makes it the one place teenagers can always go. Many branches now add a few seats, a counter by the window, a microwave, an ATM, even a printer — small comforts that turn a quick stop into a place to stay.

Then there is the cost. For a teenager with very little money, the konbini is almost uniquely welcoming: a drink costs small change, and nobody expects you to spend more. "We can sit for an hour with one bottle of tea," says Ken, 16, who meets his friends at the same store most evenings. "No one tells us to leave. At a café you feel the pressure to keep buying." That freedom from pressure is the quiet heart of the konbini's appeal.

It has even produced its own habits. In parts of Japan, gathering outside the konbini after school is common enough to be unremarkable — a small daily ritual of standing around, sharing snacks, and talking. The setting is completely ordinary, and that is exactly why it works: there is no dress code, no booking, and no reason you need to be there except that your friends are.

Not everyone sees it warmly. Some adults view groups of teenagers outside a shop as a nuisance, or worry they are "loitering" rather than buying. A few stores have removed their seating or played music to discourage young people from staying too long. Yet for many shop owners the calculation is simple: today's teenager drinking cheap tea is tomorrow's regular customer, and a steady stream of young people keeps the store busy and alive.

What the konbini offers, in the end, is not really products. It is permission — to be somewhere warm, lit and free, with the people you choose, at an hour when nowhere else will have you.

reading_passages.title: The Indoor City
reading_passages.topic: Indoor Worlds — malls as free social space (climate, free entry, social pull; mall owners divided). Good summary-skill text (three ordered reasons).
reading_passages.body:
In the hot, rainy cities of Southeast Asia, the shopping mall has become far more than a place to buy things. For many young people it is the default place to spend a free afternoon — and most of them arrive with no intention of shopping at all.

The first reason is the climate. When the temperature outside climbs past thirty-five degrees, or the afternoon rain arrives without warning, an air-conditioned mall is simply the most comfortable place to be. It costs nothing to walk in, and nobody is turned away at the door.

That free entry is the second attraction. A café expects you to buy something; a library expects silence; a mall expects neither. A teenager can sit on a bench, watch the crowds, meet friends by the fountain, and stay for hours without spending a single coin. For students with little money, few other spaces are so generous.

The third and strongest pull is social. Malls have quietly become meeting points — somewhere to see friends, be seen, and feel part of the busy life of the city. The shops are almost a backdrop. Groups gather in food courts not for the food but for the table, the air-conditioning, and each other.

Malls themselves are divided about this. Crowds of teenagers spending little can crowd out paying customers, and some centres have tried to discourage them — removing seating, or playing music they hope young people will dislike. Yet many owners take the longer view: today's window-shopping teenager is tomorrow's paying adult, and a mall full of life attracts everyone. An empty mall attracts no one.

So the indoor city endures — not because young people love shopping, but because, in a hot and expensive world, it offers something increasingly rare: a free, cool, welcoming place simply to be.

reading_passages.title: The Corner That Closed
reading_passages.topic: The Disappearing Hangout — gentrification/exclusion (an arcade closes; rent doubles; 'no loitering'; a quiet, cumulative loss). Strong for inference + writer's-attitude work.
reading_passages.body:
For three years, the small arcade on the corner of Maple Road was where Arif and his friends met after school. It was nothing special — a dozen old machines, a drinks fridge, a torn sofa — but it was warm, it was cheap, and nobody minded if you stayed for hours.

Last month, it closed. The rent had doubled, the owner explained, and a coffee chain had offered to take the space. Now the windows are papered over, and a sign promises a "premium café — opening soon."

Arif and his friends have nowhere obvious to go. The new café, when it opens, will sell coffees none of them can really afford. The mall is a bus ride away. "We're not asking for much," Arif says. "Just somewhere we're allowed to exist without buying something every twenty minutes."

His story is becoming common. Across many cities, the cheap, in-between places where young people gathered — arcades, old cafés, corner shops with a bench outside — are slowly disappearing, replaced by businesses designed for people with money to spend. The spaces that remain often quietly discourage teenagers from lingering.

None of this is dramatic. No one decided to push young people out. It happens one closed shop, one rent rise, one "no loitering" sign at a time. But the result, added up, is a city with fewer and fewer places where being young and having no money is simply allowed.

writing_model_review.task: Write a review of a place where people gather (120–150 words).
writing_model_review.model: Tucked down a side street, The Long Table is the kind of café where nobody asks you to leave. You pay by the hour, not by the cup, so its warm, low-lit ambience invites you to linger over one drink for a whole afternoon. What makes it special is the quiet — it's a genuine sanctuary during exam season. My only criticism is that seats near the window fill fast, so arrive early. It's perfect for any student who needs somewhere calm to unwind and study. I'd recommend it to anyone.
self_check: name the place and give a clear verdict.
describe the atmosphere using 2+ unit words.
give one honest criticism, not only praise.
organise my review in three clear paragraphs.
end with a recommendation and check my spelling.
